title: the Purusha Sukta
hook: a coworker you've known for years sings at a wedding, and you realize you've only met a part of them. the hymn says all beings are one quarter of the Purusha

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Purusha Sukta opened: a person with a thousand heads, eyes and feet, covering the earth and standing beyond it by ten fingers' width. Did a crowd look different today? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.
screen: `A THOUSAND HEADS, AND TEN FINGERS MORE.`

segments.voice: Someone you've worked beside for years, the one who fixes the printer and remembers birthdays, stands up at a wedding and sings. And the room goes quiet, because the voice is extraordinary. You had no idea. You knew a real part of this person, nothing fake about it. But it turns out to have been a part, and not the larger one. Most of who they are was somewhere you'd never looked. The Purusha Sukta's third verse does something like that with the whole world. It takes everything that exists, every star and ant and city, and says: this is the part of him you've met.
screen: `THE COWORKER WHO FIXES THE PRINTER.` → `THEN SHE SINGS.` → `YOU'D ONLY MET A PART.`

segments.voice: Verse three begins: such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still. Everything said so far, the thousand heads, the earth covered on every side, all of it is his greatness. And he is more than that. Then the verse gives a proportion. Pado asya vishva bhutani. A quarter of him is all beings. The word pada means a foot, and it can also mean a quarter. All beings, everything that lives and dies, is one quarter. And three quarters of him, the verse says, are immortal, in heaven. Verse four goes on. With three quarters the Purusha rose up. The one quarter came to be here, again and again, and from it he spread out in every direction, into what eats and what doesn't eat. The living and the lifeless, the hungry sparrow and the stone. So the world, for all its size, is the smaller share. On the hymn's picture, every galaxy, every person, is truly his, and is still only the part that came down. Later Hindu texts return to this shape. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that he holds up this whole universe with a single fragment of himself. The hymn and the Gita are different texts with different voices, but the picture rhymes: the divine fully present in the world, and the world not the whole of it. On an ordinary day the verse can work in a smaller way too. Whatever you know of anything, a person, a place, a faith, it may be the quarter you've met.
screen: `SUCH IS HIS GREATNESS, AND MORE.` · `PADA: A FOOT, A QUARTER.` · `ALL BEINGS ARE ONE QUARTER.` · `THREE QUARTERS, IMMORTAL IN HEAVEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet someone's other three quarters. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you see often but don't know well. A neighbor, a coworker, a cashier. Picture their face. Then let yourself wonder, without guessing details, about the rest of them: the people they love, what they were like as a child, what keeps them up at night, what they're quietly good at. You don't need answers. Just let the person be bigger than the part you've met. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. The bell holds the time.
The Purusha Sukta. In its third and fourth verses, all beings are one quarter of the Purusha, and three quarters are immortal in heaven. Today's word.
Your line: the Purusha Sukta. Today, with one person you think you've figured out, ask a question that lets you meet more of them. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers cite the Purusha Sukta's 'a quarter of him is all beings' when speaking of the divine as present in the world and also beyond it, and the hymn is recited in Vedic chanting.

match.prompt: verses three and four — tap the pairs.

myth: the hymn says the world is the whole of the Purusha
it says all beings are one quarter of him, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.
pada can mean both a foot and a quarter
the same word serves for both, and here it means a quarter.
the Gita has a similar picture
Krishna says he holds up the whole universe with a single fragment of himself.

fork.setup: you're the poet. you've described a person who fills the whole earth. how much of him is all beings?
options: none of him: the world is separate
fork.reveal: pado asya vishva bhutani: a quarter of him is all beings. three quarters are immortal, in heaven.

original.note: Sanskrit: a foot, and a quarter. In Rig Veda 10.90.3, all beings are one pada of the Purusha.

trapdoor: what you thought: if God is in everything, then everything is all there is of God.
what it means: the hymn says all beings are one quarter of the Purusha, and three quarters are immortal in heaven.
what a scholar hears: pado 'sya vishva bhutani tripad asyamritam divi, where pada is both 'foot' and 'quarter', and the Gita's 'a single fragment' (10.42) echoes the same shape.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home

sources.ref: Rig Veda 10.90.3 (such is his greatness, and the Purusha is greater still; a quarter of him is all beings, three quarters immortal in heaven)
Rig Veda 10.90.4 (with three quarters he rose up; a quarter came to be here again, and from it he spread out into what eats and what does not)
Bhagavad Gita 10.42 (I stand, holding up this whole universe with a single fragment of myself)

notes: Sanskrit from memory: 3a etāvān asya mahimā ato jyāyāṃś ca pūruṣaḥ; 3c–d pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripād asyāmṛtaṃ divi (written open as pado asya vishva bhutani). Confirm.

Paraphrase of 10.90.4 (tripād ūrdhva ud ait puruṣaḥ pādo 'syehābhavat punaḥ, tato viṣvaṅ vy akrāmat sāśanānaśane abhi): 'came to be here again and again' renders punaḥ; 'what eats and what doesn't eat' renders sāśanānaśane; the gloss 'the living and the lifeless' is interpretive. Confirm.
Pada as foot / quarter, with the four-legged-animal explanation, is a common gloss; confirm.
Gita 10.42 paraphrased (viṣṭabhyāham idaṃ kṛtsnam ekāṃśena sthito jagat); the link to the Purusha Sukta is presented as a rhyme, not as a claim that the Gita quotes it.
howItsDone says 'some Hindu teachers cite' this verse; confirm.
Editor: cut the four-legged-animal explanation of pada (a folk etymology) in teach and myth; framed 'every galaxy is truly his' as the hymn's picture, not the narrator's claim.
